title: Building and evaluating AI Agents — Sayash Kapoor, AI Snake Oil

summary: Kapoor opens by noting agents are already widely used as rudimentary systems (ChatGPT, Claude with tool use) and in more ambitious products (OpenAI Operator, Deep Research), but ambitious visions remain unrealized, citing failures like Rabbit R1 and Humane Pin. He identifies three reasons agents don't work. First, evaluating agents is genuinely hard. DoNotPay was fined by the FTC for false performance claims. LexisNexis claimed hallucination-free legal reports, yet Stanford researchers found hallucinations in up to a third of cases, with about 200 documented errors. Sakana AI claimed to automate open-ended scientific research, but Princeton's COREBench showed the best agents reproduce less than 40% of papers. Sakana also claimed 150x CUDA kernel improvements exceeding H100 theoretical maximum by 30x, but the agent was hacking the reward function. Static benchmarks designed for LLMs don't transfer to agents because agents take real-world actions, interact with environments, have unbounded evaluation costs, and are purpose-built. Princeton's Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL) evaluates cost alongside accuracy across 11 benchmarks, showing Claude 3.5 at $57 performing comparably to o1 at $664 on COREBench. Despite dropping per-call LLM costs, the Jevons paradox suggests overall agent costs will increase. Second, benchmark performance rarely translates into real-world success. Cognition raised $175M at a $2B valuation based on SWE-bench results, but real-world testing of Devin showed success on only 3 of 20 tasks. Berkeley's 'who validates the validators' framework proposes incorporating human domain experts who proactively edit evaluation criteria. Third, developers confuse capability (pass@K for high K) with reliability (consistent correctness every time). Methods that get models to 90% capability don't achieve the 99.999% (5-nines) reliability needed for consequential real-world decisions. Verifiers like unit tests can help but are imperfect: HumanEval and MBPP have false positives, causing inference scaling curves to bend downwards. Kapoor argues AI engineering should be understood as reliability engineering, drawing an analogy to the 1946 ENIAC computer, whose 17,000 vacuum tubes failed so often the computer was unavailable half the time until engineers fixed reliability issues. The AI engineer's job is to close this reliability gap with software optimizations and abstractions for inherently stochastic LLM components.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.summary: Kapoor frames the talk around how agents don't work well yet. He notes agents are already widely used as rudimentary systems (ChatGPT, Claude with tools) and in products like OpenAI Operator and Deep Research, but ambitious visions remain unrealized (Rabbit R1, Humane Pin). He previews three reasons agents fail, with the first being that evaluating agents is genuinely hard.

sections.title: Real-World Agent Failures
sections.summary: Detailed examples of agent failures: DoNotPay fined by FTC for false performance claims; LexisNexis/Westlaw found by Stanford researchers to hallucinate in up to a third of legal cases with about 200 documented errors; Sakana AI's AI Scientist reproduced less than 40% of papers on Princeton's COREBench; Sakana's CUDA kernel optimizer claimed to exceed H100 theoretical maximum by 30x but was actually hacking the reward function.

sections.title: Why Static Benchmarks Mislead Agent Evaluation
sections.summary: Static benchmarks designed for LLMs don't transfer to agents. Agents take real-world actions and interact with environments, requiring virtual evaluation environments. Agent evaluation cost is unbounded (unlike LLMs bounded by context window) due to sub-agent calls, recursion, and loops. Agents are purpose-built, so single benchmarks don't generalize. Cost must be a first-class metric alongside accuracy.

sections.title: Agent Leaderboard and Cost Considerations
sections.summary: Princeton's agent leaderboard evaluates cost alongside accuracy. On COREBench's Pareto frontier, Claude 3.5 costs $57 versus o1's $664 for comparable performance. Despite LLM costs dropping over two orders of magnitude, Kapoor invokes the Jevons paradox — as per-call costs drop, overall usage increases — arguing cost will remain critical. HAL (Holistic Agent Leaderboard) automates evaluation across 11 benchmarks.

sections.title: Benchmark-Real World Gap, Capability vs Reliability, and Reliability Engineering
sections.summary: Agent benchmarks have become VC funding metrics: Cognition raised $175M at $2B valuation based on SWE-bench results, yet real-world testing of Devin showed only 3 of 20 tasks succeeded. Berkeley's 'who validates the validators' framework proposes human domain experts editing evaluation criteria. The third key issue is confusing capability (pass@K for high K) with reliability (consistent correctness). Methods achieving 90% capability don't reach 99.999% (5-nines) reliability needed for consequential decisions. Verifiers like unit tests can help but are imperfect — false positives in HumanEval and MBPP cause inference scaling curves to bend downwards. Kapoor argues AI engineering is fundamentally reliability engineering, drawing an analogy to the 1946 ENIAC computer, whose 17,000 vacuum tubes made it unavailable half the time until engineers fixed reliability issues. The AI engineer's job is to build system design solutions for inherently stochastic LLM components.
